title: Govern disaster recovery activation and coordination
summary: Disaster recovery process governance gives people authority, sequence, communication, and evidence when an event requires coordinated restoration of prioritized services.
outcome: Given a disruptive event, coordinate declaration, response, personnel, communications, assessment, training, and lessons ownership without confusing technical recovery with business acceptance.
managerMindset: During a disaster, make authority, priorities, people, communications, and evidence explicit before the pressure of restoration creates unsafe improvisation.

sections.title: Declare the event and establish control
sections.body: A DR process translates criteria into an accountable declaration, notification, assessment, response, recovery, and transition sequence. Define who can declare, what evidence or thresholds trigger escalation, which services and dependencies are prioritized, where decisions are recorded, and how emergency access and changes are governed. Response may include life safety, stabilization, containment, alternate processing, supplier coordination, and preservation of evidence. The process should support incomplete information without allowing every team to make conflicting recovery decisions.
keyPoints: Declaration authority and activation criteria should be defined before an event.
Technical and business priorities must be reconciled through a documented decision authority.
Emergency actions still need traceability, access control, and later review.

sections.title: Coordinate people, communication, and readiness
sections.body: Assign recovery, technical, business, facilities, communications, supplier, security, and safety responsibilities with primary and alternate contacts. Communication methods should account for unavailable networks, confidentiality, authentication, message approval, stakeholder needs, regulators, customers, and staff welfare. Training and awareness make plans executable: people need role practice, contact updates, decision authority, safe work instructions, and escalation routes. Capture lessons from exercises and events with owners and deadlines rather than relying on a retrospective conversation.
keyPoints: A contact list is not a communication plan unless channels and fallbacks are tested.
Personnel safety and role clarity constrain what recovery actions are acceptable.
Training evidence should show that designated people can perform their decisions, not only that they received a document.

workedExamples.title: Regional identity outage
workedExamples.situation: A regional outage affects identity, network, and application services. The operations lead wants to declare DR, while the business owner has not confirmed which customer functions must be restored first.
workedExamples.reasoning: Use the defined declaration criteria, record the uncertainty, activate the recovery authority, and obtain the business priority decision while technical teams assess dependencies. Use out-of-band communication if the normal channel is affected, restrict emergency access, and document the assumptions that will be revisited during restoration.

distinctions.difference: A DR declaration activates coordinated recovery governance for a disruptive event; incident escalation may raise response authority without invoking the full recovery process.
Response stabilizes people, information, and conditions and coordinates decisions; restoration rebuilds or returns prioritized service under acceptance criteria.
Training develops role-specific ability to perform; awareness communicates expectations and helps people recognize and escalate concerns.

misconceptions.misconception: The technical team can declare and prioritize DR alone.
misconceptions.correction: Technical evidence informs the decision, but business authority and continuity priorities determine which services and risks are accepted.

misconceptions.misconception: A mass email is a crisis communication plan.
misconceptions.correction: A plan needs authenticated channels, fallbacks, approval, audience-specific content, confidentiality, and tested contact ownership.

recallChecks.answer: The conditions, authority, services or scope, initial evidence, notification path, and decision record for declaring or escalating recovery.
Tested alternate channels, authentication and confidentiality, message ownership and approval, stakeholder coverage, and fallback procedures.
That designated people can perform their roles, make decisions, use communications, and escalate safely under realistic constraints.

scenarioSeeds.scenario: The primary crisis bridge is unavailable, and a supplier requests privileged credentials by email to accelerate recovery.
scenarioSeeds.decision: Use the approved out-of-band channel, verify supplier identity and authority, issue bounded emergency access through the controlled process, and record the decision.
scenarioSeeds.why: Pressure and unavailable systems do not remove the need for authenticated communication and least privilege.

visualLearningContract.teachingQuestion: Who declares, restores, validates, accepts, and transitions DR service?
visualLearningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.
visualLearningContract.retrievalPrompt: Name objective, dependency, owner, evidence, acceptance.
visualLearningContract.textFallback:
Disaster Recovery Process: The governed sequence that converts an approved recovery strategy into declaration, notification, assessment, restoration, validation, business acceptance, and return-to-normal activities. Decision: Approve the process when it assigns accountable roles, activation criteria, communications, dependencies, recovery objectives, and exercise evidence. Failure: An unowned or untested process produces delayed escalation, conflicting actions, or restoration that cannot be accepted safely.
DR Declaration: An authorized decision that a disruptive event meets predefined criteria for activating DR governance and recovery resources. Decision: Declare when verified impact, scope, recovery-objective risk, and designated authority meet the plan’s activation threshold. Failure: Ambiguous authority or thresholds delay escalation or trigger costly recovery without sufficient evidence.
DR Roles: Named primary and alternate responsibilities for technical recovery, business decisions, facilities, security, communications, suppliers, and safety. Decision: Assign roles before disruption; validate contactability, authority, dependencies, and handoffs in exercises. Failure: A generic team list leaves essential decisions or handoffs unowned when a primary person or network is unavailable.
Recovery Team: The coordinated people who execute technical and business recovery tasks under the assigned recovery authority. Decision: Staff the team for the affected services, skills, alternates, supplier dependencies, and safe working conditions. Failure: Insufficient skills, absent alternates, or uncoordinated teams can restore components while leaving the service unusable.
Crisis Communications: Controlled, audience-specific communications that keep staff, leaders, customers, suppliers, and authorities informed using resilient channels. Decision: Use approved messages, owners, cadence, escalation paths, and alternate channels appropriate to the event and audience. Failure: Unverified or inconsistent messages create unsafe actions, regulatory exposure, or loss of stakeholder trust.
Damage Assessment: A rapid, evidence-based determination of affected people, facilities, systems, data, identities, dependencies, and recovery-option viability. Decision: Assess before selecting restoration actions; preserve evidence and update scope as facts change. Failure: Restoring on unverified assumptions can spread compromise, overlook dependencies, or choose an unavailable alternate strategy.
DR Training: Role-specific preparation that enables people to execute recovery procedures, communications, safety actions, and decision handoffs. Decision: Train before an event and refresh after role, system, supplier, or plan changes; verify with exercises. Failure: Reading a plan does not demonstrate that personnel can coordinate safely under time pressure.
DR Lessons Learned: Evidence-supported findings from events or exercises that lead to owned corrective actions, plan updates, and retests. Decision: Record observed versus expected results, assign owner/due date/evidence, then retest material changes. Failure: Closing an exercise with an attendance record or unowned notes repeats the same readiness gap.
Recovery Authority: The delegated decision right to activate DR, commit resources, accept service restoration, manage exceptions, and end recovery status. Decision: Document authority limits, alternates, business acceptance roles, and escalation paths before disruption. Failure: A technical team must not silently substitute for business acceptance or commit resources outside its authority.
